- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

When a session crashes mid-task, its full transcript is on disk at
`/home/runner/.claude/projects/-home-runner-workspace/<session-id>.jsonl` (mirrored under
`.claude-home/projects/`). Newest file by mtime is usually the crashed one.

**Why:** on 2026-08-15 a crashed review had already done 22 minutes of expensive work —
719 tests, a 96-visit browser sweep, a live API sweep, a forged-admin proof. All of it was
recoverable in ~5 tool calls instead of being repeated.

**How to apply:**
- Parse the JSONL line-by-line as JSON. `type:"assistant"` entries hold `message.content[]`
  with `text` blocks (the narrative — read these first, they summarize every finding) and
  `tool_use` blocks. `type:"user"` entries hold `tool_result` blocks keyed by
  `tool_use_id`.
- Build an index mapping `tool_use.id` → ordinal, then dump the results you want by ordinal.
  Listing all `tool_use` calls with a one-line description first makes it obvious which
  results are worth pulling.
- Filter `<system-reminder>` and `<local-command-caveat>` blocks out of user text to find
  the real original prompt.
- **Then invert the lesson:** on any long task, write findings to a real file on disk as you
  go, not just into context. The 2026-08-15 review kept
  `docs/REVIEW-2026-08-15-full-app-review.md` updated incrementally for exactly this reason.

Reviewed properly. There are real defects — the gate was green because nothing tested for these.

## Must fix — correctness

**1. The scope filter uses the wrong join, and disagrees with property-home.**

Phase 9 hand-rolled its filter (`property-terminal.tsx:216-224`) as *active tenant at that address → their invoice IDs*. But `property-home` scopes via the shared helper `filterByProperty` (`client/src/lib/property-dashboard-data.ts:117`), which matches on **the invoice's own `propertyAddress`**, falling back to the tenant's. The server sends that field on every invoice (`server/routes.ts:7433-7441`), and it looks tenants up with `getTenantProfile` regardless of archived status.

Two consequences, both money-visible:
- An **archived** tenant's unpaid invoice counts in "all properties" but is dropped from *every* per-property scope — so the per-property figures no longer sum to the portfolio total. That's the tenant who left owing you rent, disappearing from the one view you'd use to chase it. The model file deliberately preserves those rows (`property-terminal-model.ts:99-100` — *"the server's enriched name survives archiving"*), so Phase 9 works against an explicit design decision.
- Two chips that look identical on two screens can report different numbers for the same property.

Fix: use `filterByProperty`. It's the cause-and-cure of the whole finding.

**2. The automation panel ignores the scope** — and the gate's own screenshot proves it. `liveSchedules` (`:491`) is never filtered by `propFilter`. In `desktop-12-scoped.png`, scoped to **12 Kauri Road**, RECURRING RENT still lists **Mia Chen**, who the fixture puts at *5 Bellbird Rise*. I took the screenshot as evidence the feature worked and didn't read the right-hand panel.

## Should fix — port fidelity

**3. The port dropped `text-transform:lowercase`.** `.ph-scope` and `.ph-scope-opt` both carry it (`property-home.tsx:608,611`); `.pt-scope-opt` doesn't. The entire terminal is lowercase — "all properties", "outstanding rent", "rent request" — and the menu now renders "12 Kauri Road", "5 Bellbird Rise", "88 Harbour View" capitalised right below the lowercase "all properties". Clearly visible in the screenshot above. The plan said *port* these styles; this is a port error, not a deviation.

**4. `propFilter` never resets.** If the last active tenant at the scoped property is archived, the chip keeps displaying that address, every list goes empty, and the address is gone from the menu — no way back except picking "all properties".

## Worth noting — inherited, not a regression

**5. No outside-click or Escape dismissal.** There are zero `addEventListener` calls in the whole file, so this matches the existing popover pattern. But it bites harder here: the menu is up to 260px tall and, as the screenshot shows, **covers the outstanding-rent hero figure** — the primary number on the screen — and you can only get it back by re-clicking the chip or picking an option.

One genuine judgment call before I fix these:

The automation rail mode is gone — `Mode` is down to five, the rail to five buttons, and the 190-line panel with it. The panel scrolls internally and tops out at 652px.

**No red or green anywhere in it.** The destructive confirm carries weight as a filled blue chip rather than a red one, and a schedule's active/paused state reads from the word's weight and opacity. Status dots, split badge and mark-paid tick are untouched, per your "only what I'm touching now" — and I've saved the rule to memory so it isn't relearned next session.

One thing worth knowing: every existing automation test passed through the move **unchanged**, because the disclosure kept the old rail button's accessible name. That's a silent-regression trap, so I added a test pinning the rail to its five modes — otherwise the tab could come back and nothing would fail.

## Three commits this session

- `cedef72` — Phase 9 scope chip, closing the parity plan at 9/9
- `b083838` — the review defects, chiefly the scope join that made archived tenants' debt vanish from every per-property view while still counting in the portfolio total
- `64633ad` — this change

## Still open for you

Yesterday's crash is explained, and not by the container restart I first offered: `527663fc` sat at 0% CPU logging *"a second chromium group spawned ~2 min in"* while `76d1755e` ran its verifier. Two sessions driving headless chromium at one dev server deadlocked each other.

Which matters now, because **three Claude sessions are live on this branch** — the other two committed `2d3b24c` and `4f6ae67` (mobile dock reservation, Phase A) while I was working. No conflicts, no cross-contamination, and I've kept every commit staged by explicit path. But browser gates from two sessions at once will hang again, so it's worth coordinating who runs them.
